passage: Experts who manage risk often speak of the public with weary patience. People, they observe, fear the wrong things. They worry about a nuclear plant that has never harmed anyone in the district while driving, without a second thought, along a road that kills several of their neighbours every year. They demand inquiries after a single dramatic accident and shrug at the steady toll of falls in the home. On this account the task of policy is to correct a problem of perception: to replace vivid fears with sober numbers, so that resources follow expected deaths rather than headlines.

There is something to this, but less than its confidence suggests. When people are asked to describe what makes a hazard frightening, their answers are not random. Risks feel worse when they are imposed rather than chosen, when they could kill many people at once rather than a few at a time, when their effects are delayed or invisible, and when those who create them are not those who bear them. None of these features is captured by a count of expected fatalities, yet none of them is obviously foolish. A person who accepts the dangers of rock climbing but objects to a factory releasing an untested chemical into the river is not confused about arithmetic. She is drawing a distinction between a risk she has consented to and one that has been placed on her by others, and that distinction is a moral one that most legal systems also recognise.

Seen this way, the gap between expert and lay rankings of hazards is partly a disagreement about what the question is. The expert asks how many people will die; the citizen asks, in addition, whether the arrangement that produces those deaths is fair, controllable and worthy of trust. To call the second question irrational is to settle a dispute about values by redescribing it as a dispute about facts.

None of this makes dread a reliable guide. The features that make a hazard feel threatening can be manufactured by vivid reporting, and fear can drive choices that increase the very danger it is meant to avoid. If travellers abandon aircraft for cars after a well-publicised crash, they may exchange a small risk for a larger one without noticing the trade. The sensible response is neither to dismiss public fear as noise nor to treat it as a verdict. It is to take it apart: to ask which of its components reflect values that deserve a hearing in policy, and which reflect only the salience of a recent and alarming image.

passage: When two experts disagree about a question the rest of us cannot assess, it can seem that the layperson has only two options: to become an expert herself, or to pick a side at random. Neither is attractive. The first is usually impossible within the time available, and the second makes a mockery of the idea that belief should answer to evidence. But the dilemma is false. Although the layperson cannot judge the dispute directly, she can often judge the disputants, and judgements of that kind can be reasonable even when the subject matter remains opaque to her.

Several kinds of evidence are available. She can ask whether either expert has a record of predictions that can be checked, and how those predictions fared. She can ask whether one of them stands to gain from being believed, through money, reputation or loyalty to an institution. She can ask how the rest of the field divides, bearing in mind that a majority counts for more when its members reached their views independently than when they all learned them from the same teacher. None of these questions requires understanding the dispute itself. Each concerns the circumstances in which a claim is advanced rather than its technical content, and each can be answered, at least roughly, by an attentive citizen with no specialised training whatever.

One tempting source of evidence is less useful than it looks. Laypeople often favour the expert who argues more fluently, answers objections more quickly and seems more at ease. Yet these are skills of performance, and they are only loosely connected with being right. A careful scientist may hedge, pause and admit uncertainties that a confident charlatan would brush aside, and an audience that rewards confidence is, in effect, rewarding the very habit that should make it suspicious. The difficulty is compounded by the fact that public debate, with its brief exchanges and its appetite for memorable phrases, is arranged almost entirely so as to display performance, and so to favour the disputant who has mastered it.

It would be a mistake to conclude that the layperson's position is comfortable. Track records are often unavailable for the questions that matter most, interests can be hidden, and a field can be captured by a fashion that makes its consensus less independent than it appears. The indirect methods narrow the range of reasonable belief; they rarely close it. Still, a choice made on such grounds is not a coin toss, and treating it as one hands an advantage to whoever is most willing to exploit the public's sense of helplessness.

passage: In a number of countries a newborn cannot simply be given whatever name the parents choose. A registrar may refuse a name that is judged offensive, that does not clearly indicate whether the bearer is male or female, that is spelt in a way the national orthography does not allow, or that does not appear on an official list. Defenders of such rules usually present them as a modest form of child protection. Parents, the argument runs, are fallible and sometimes vain; the child carries the name for a lifetime and had no say in choosing it; and the state, which already requires that children be schooled and vaccinated, may reasonably insist that they not be saddled with a label that will invite mockery.

There is something to this. A name is not a private ornament but a tool that other people use, and a name that cannot be pronounced, written on a form or read out in a classroom without laughter does impose a cost on the person who bears it. Cases in which parents have tried to register a brand name, a string of numbers or an insult are real enough, and few people would object to a registrar declining them. If the rules went no further than this, they would hardly be worth arguing about.

But they usually go much further, and the further they go, the less work the child-protection argument does. A rule that a name must indicate the bearer's sex protects no child from ridicule; it protects a social expectation. A rule that a name may use only the letters of the national alphabet does not shield the daughter of immigrant parents from mockery; if anything, it obliges her to carry an altered spelling of her grandmother's name, one that marks her at every roll call as someone whose family had to be corrected. An approved list, finally, protects children chiefly from novelty, and novelty is not a harm. Many names now regarded as solid and traditional were once eccentric inventions, and a register that had frozen the stock of names a century ago would have prevented most of them.

What the stricter rules actually defend, then, is the stock of names itself, treated as a piece of national heritage that private choices might erode. That is a coherent aim, and some will think it a worthy one. It should, however, be argued for openly as cultural policy and weighed against the interest parents have in naming their children as their own traditions require, rather than smuggled in under the language of protecting the young. A state that wishes to guard children from cruel names needs a short list of what is forbidden, not a long list of what is allowed.

passage: Boredom is usually described as a kind of emptiness, the feeling of having nothing to feel. On this view it is a residue, what remains when interest drains away, and the natural response is to fill the space with whatever is at hand, much as one might fill an awkward silence with remarks about the weather. The description is understandable, since boredom rarely announces any object of its own, but it gets the state almost exactly backwards. Boredom is not an absence. It is an active and often insistent signal that the activity in front of us is failing to engage the capacities we have available, and it exists to make us do something about that.

The comparison with other unpleasant states is instructive. Hunger is disagreeable, but nobody concludes from this that hunger is a defect; its discomfort is the means by which it gets us to eat. Boredom works in a similar way. A person bored by a repetitive clerical task does not merely register that the task is dull; she feels restless, glances at the clock, begins to imagine alternatives. The unpleasantness is doing work. It pushes attention away from a situation that offers too little and towards a search for one that offers more, whether that means a harder problem, a different companion or simply a walk.

None of this implies that boredom is always benign. A signal is useful only when there is some way to act on it, and many situations offer none. The patient in a waiting room, the passenger on a delayed train and the worker who cannot leave a monotonous post all receive the message without being able to respond, and in such cases boredom curdles into frustration or something close to despair. There are also signs that people will sometimes reach for almost any stimulation rather than endure an unoccupied mind, even stimulation they would otherwise find unpleasant. The signal, in other words, can be loud enough to drive choices that serve no one, and a theory of boredom that celebrated it without reservation would be as misleading as one that dismissed it.

What follows is a reason to be wary of the most popular remedy. If boredom is a message about the fit between a person and an activity, then an endless supply of small distractions does not answer the message; it merely muffles it. Someone who reaches for a screen at every lull may never feel bored for long, but may also never learn what the boredom was pointing at: a job that has stopped stretching them, a routine that has outlived its purpose, a curiosity that has gone unfed. The more useful question, when boredom arrives, is not how to make it stop but what it is about.

passage: A man resolves to give up sweets, believes sincerely that he should, and then, at the end of a long and exhausting day, eats the cake anyway. The episode is so ordinary that its strangeness is easy to miss. If he really judged that refusing was better, what moved him to do otherwise? One very old answer is that nothing did: no one knowingly chooses the worse course, and the man must have ceased to believe, at least temporarily, that refusing was better. Most people find this answer too clever by half. They are convinced that they have acted against their own considered judgement, and they describe the experience in the vocabulary of force, of being overcome by something stronger than resolution.

The popular picture that develops from this description treats the will as a kind of muscle. Judgement indicates the direction, and the will either possesses the strength to follow or it does not; lapses are failures of strength, to be corrected by training, rest or improved nutrition. The picture has the merit of matching how lapses feel, and it explains why they cluster at the end of tiring days. But it makes the lapse strangely external to the person, as though desire were a weight imposed from outside and the self merely a lifter who happened to be exhausted that particular evening.

Closer examination of such moments suggests a different interpretation. The man with the cake does not usually go on thinking, clearly and vividly, that he should refuse while his hand reaches out. Instead his attention narrows: the considerations favouring refusal, which seemed compelling in the morning, become abstract and distant, while the cake is immediate, particular and present. He does not abandon his judgement so much as stop looking at it. On this interpretation the lapse is neither a mere deficiency of strength nor a simple change of mind but a failure to keep one's own reasons in view.

This does not mean that fatigue is irrelevant, or that every lapse is a matter of attention; some temptations are simply strong, and some people are considerably more depleted than others. But the attentional account has a practical advantage. If lapses were exclusively failures of strength, the only remedy would be additional strength. If they are often failures of attention, the remedy can be arrangement: keeping one's reasons concrete, placing the cake out of sight, deciding in advance what one will do when the moment arrives. People who manage their weaknesses successfully tend to do precisely this, and the muscle picture has trouble explaining why such strategies work.

passage: For much of modern political thought, to be free has meant to be left alone. On this view a person's liberty is diminished whenever someone interferes with her choices, by force, by threat or by the closing off of options, and it is enlarged whenever such interference is removed. The view has the merit of simplicity, and it gives a clear direction to political argument: other things being equal, less interference means more freedom. An older tradition, recently revived, holds that this account misses something essential. What makes a person unfree, it says, is not interference as such but dependence on the will of another who could interfere at pleasure, whether or not he ever does.

The point is easiest to see in a case where the two accounts come apart. Imagine a tenant whose lease allows the landlord to evict her at any time and for any reason, and whose landlord happens to be a mild man who has never troubled anyone. On the non-interference view the tenant is perfectly free, since nobody is stopping her from doing anything. Yet she knows her position. She will think twice before complaining about a broken boiler, she will keep her opinion of the landlord to herself, and she may find herself anticipating his preferences in matters he has never raised. The absence of interference in her life is not evidence that she is free; it may be, in part, an effect of her unfreedom, since a person who must stay in another's good graces learns to make interference unnecessary. The rival tradition calls her condition domination, and it defines freedom as the absence of domination.

The shift has striking consequences. Interference, on this view, does not always reduce freedom. A law that restrains me, but that I and others like me can contest through courts, elections and other channels that force those who make it to take our interests into account, does not subject me to anyone's arbitrary will, and so does not make me less free, even though it limits what I may do. Conversely, a benevolent ruler who chooses to interfere very little may still leave his subjects unfree, because what they are permitted to do depends on his continued goodwill.

Critics reply that the notion of arbitrary power is too elastic to do the work asked of it. Almost every relationship, from employment to marriage to the ordinary dealings of neighbours, contains some capacity of one party to make the other's life worse. If all such capacities count as domination, then domination is everywhere and the concept loses its edge; if only some do, we need a criterion, and the obvious candidates seem to smuggle back the very judgements about interference that the theory hoped to avoid. Defenders answer that power is arbitrary when it is not forced to track the interests of those subject to it, and that whether it is so forced is a question about institutions: about rights of exit, of appeal and of collective voice.

This answer is better than the critics allow, but it is not quite enough to turn non-domination into a measure. It tells us where to look rather than how much freedom we will find there. That may be its real value. The non-interference view, by counting acts, trains attention on what happens; the rival view, by asking about standing, trains it on what could happen, and on the structures that make some things unthinkable to attempt. Even if it cannot yield a neat scale, the second view identifies a kind of unfreedom that a tally of interferences would never register.

passage: There are two familiar ways of misunderstanding pilgrimage, and they are mirror images of each other. The first treats the journey as mere transport: what matters is arrival at the shrine, the sight of the image or the relic, the bath in the river, and the road is simply the price paid to get there. The second, popular among those who walk old pilgrim routes for reasons they would not call religious, reverses the emphasis. The destination, on this view, is almost a pretext; the real value lies in the walking itself, the days of effort, the strangers met on the way, the slow emptying of the mind.

Each view captures something that pilgrims genuinely report, but both detach two elements that draw their meaning from each other, and neither can be made intelligible without the other. The hardships of the road are not valuable in the abstract. Blistered feet on a hiking holiday are an inconvenience; the same blisters on the way to a sacred place become an offering, a sign of seriousness, a story to be told on return. What converts them is the fixed point towards which they are directed. Equally, the shrine does not possess its full weight for the pilgrim independently of the effort spent reaching it. A visitor who arrives by car on a whim may see exactly what the pilgrim sees and still not have had the pilgrim's experience.

The history of easier travel bears this interdependence out in an unexpected way, and it is worth dwelling on because it runs against a natural expectation. One might have predicted that when roads, railways and buses made distant shrines accessible within hours, the effortful element would simply vanish. In many places it has instead been reintroduced by choice. Pilgrims who have covered most of the distance in comfort often leave the vehicle to walk the final stretch, sometimes barefoot, sometimes on their knees. The effort has been condensed rather than abandoned, as though people sense that arrival without cost would not count as arrival at all.

None of this means that the walker who sets out with no particular reverence is deceived about what he finds. Long days on foot do change people, and the change can be real without being religious. But it is worth noticing what such a walker relinquishes, perhaps without realising it, when the destination becomes optional rather than obligatory. The pilgrim cannot decide halfway that another town would do just as well, and that inability is part of what lends the road its gravity. A journey that could end anywhere is a fine thing; it is simply a different thing from one that must end in a particular place.

passage: A curious reversal has taken place in the market for handmade goods. For most of history, the aim of a skilled potter or weaver was regularity: bowls that stacked, threads of even thickness, a pattern that repeated without drift. Irregularity was the mark of an apprentice or of a hurried job, and the master's pride lay in eliminating it. Today, by contrast, the small wobble in a glaze or the slight lean of a hand-thrown cup is what many buyers are paying for. It has become the proof that a person, and not a machine, was involved.

The trouble with this proof is that it can be forged. A machine that can make a perfect cup can be programmed to make an imperfect one, and to vary the imperfection from piece to piece so that no two look alike. Tableware with deliberately uneven rims and glazes is already produced in quantity, and an ordinary buyer cannot tell it from the real thing. If what we value in the handmade is irregularity as such, then the handmade has no defence against its imitation, and the premium paid for it is a premium paid for a story.

But irregularity was never the point, and treating it as the point misunderstands what a craftsperson does. A turner working a piece of wood meets a knot, a change in the grain, a softer patch, and alters the cut to suit it; a weaver feels the tension of the warp change with the damp in the air and corrects for it. The handmade object is the record of many such small judgements, each a response to the particular material in front of the maker. Its variations, where they occur, are traces of that responsiveness, not ornaments added afterwards. passage: Every generation of reformers discovers that words wear out. A term introduced to replace a cruder one, chosen precisely because it carried none of the old contempt, acquires that contempt within a few decades, and a new term is proposed to replace it in turn. Students of language sometimes call this cycle a treadmill, and the image is apt: a great deal of effort is expended, and the speaker seems to remain in the same place. Words for bodily functions, for old age, for poverty and for conditions of the mind have all passed through several such rotations, each new coinage arriving clean and departing stained.

The usual explanation is that the stain was never in the word. Attitudes towards the thing named are what give a word its colouring, and so long as those attitudes persist, any word that reliably points at the thing will soon absorb them. On this view the replacement of terms is a kind of displacement activity, a way of feeling that something has been done while the underlying attitude goes untouched. Critics who hold this view tend to conclude that the whole enterprise of renaming is futile, and some go further and call it dishonest, since the fresh term flatters the speaker as much as it spares the listener.

The first half of this argument seems to me largely right, and the second half too hasty. It is true that a new word cannot by itself change what people feel about the thing it names. But the treadmill is not simply a record of failure. A replacement term, for the years before it darkens, often gives people a way of speaking about a subject without signalling contempt, and in that interval conversations become possible that were not possible before. A parent can ask a teacher about a child's difficulty in terms that do not insult the child; an official form can ask about a condition without reading like an accusation. These are small goods, but they are not nothing, and they are purchased cheaply.

What the treadmill does show is that renaming cannot carry the whole burden of reform. A society that changes its vocabulary for poverty while leaving the poor exactly as they were will find that its new word sours as fast as the old one, and perhaps faster, since the gap between the gentle name and the harsh reality invites irony. The cycle slows, where it slows at all, when the thing named stops being a mark of shame. The word then has nothing to absorb. Renaming is best understood not as a substitute for that change but as a temporary courtesy that can accompany it.

passage: Inquiries into industrial disasters have a way of finding a culprit. An operator ignored a warning, an inspector signed a form he had not read, a manager overruled an engineer whose objections were inconvenient. Such findings are rarely false, but they are often beside the point, because they treat as a single failure of judgement what was in fact the end of a long and orderly process. Many organisations do not stumble into catastrophe; they walk towards it by steps that each seemed reasonable at the time.

Consider a hypothetical chemical plant whose procedures say that a certain vessel must be shut down if its pressure exceeds a stated limit. One night the gauge registers a reading marginally above the permitted limit. Shutting down would be expensive, the excess is small, and the engineers on duty judge, correctly as it turns out, that the vessel is in no danger. Nothing untoward happens, and the next time the reading creeps over the limit there is a precedent, which makes the decision considerably easier. After a dozen such nights the limit has quietly moved: the written figure still stands in the manual, but the working figure, the one people actually act on, is higher. No one decided to change it. The change was made by the accumulated absence of harm.

This is what makes the process so difficult to detect from within the organisation itself. Each step is defended by evidence, and the evidence is genuine, for the vessel really did not fail. What is mistaken is the inference drawn from it, that a risk which has not yet produced harm has thereby been shown to be small. Success becomes a reason for confidence, and confidence a reason to look less closely, so that the organisation's sense of its own safety grows at the same rate as its actual exposure to danger. By the time an outsider asks why the plant routinely runs above its limit, the question sounds naive, because everyone inside knows that it always has.

It does not follow that every departure from the rules is a step towards disaster. Written procedures are drafted in advance by people who cannot foresee every situation, and an organisation whose staff never deviated from them would be unable to adapt; much good practice begins as a sensible exception. The danger lies not in deviation itself but in deviation that is never recognised as such. A departure that is noticed, argued over and formally adopted is a decision; one that simply accumulates is drift, and drift answers to no one.

passage: Among the arguments made for nuclear deterrence, the strongest is also the simplest: when two states can each destroy the other, neither can hope to gain from a general war, and so neither starts one. Whatever its moral costs, a balance of terror of this kind has a claim to have kept the largest powers from fighting each other directly for a long time. But the logic that makes the largest war unthinkable may make smaller ones more thinkable, and this possibility, sometimes called the stability-instability paradox, deserves more attention than the reassuring half of the argument usually receives.

The reasoning runs as follows. If both sides are confident that neither will ever risk a nuclear exchange, then each can assume that a limited clash, whether a border skirmish, a proxy war or a raid by irregular forces, will stay limited. The fear that once restrained such ventures, the fear that they might spiral into catastrophe, is weakened precisely by the confidence that catastrophe will be avoided. Stability at the top of the ladder of escalation thus loosens the rungs near the bottom. A state that would never dare a full invasion may feel free to probe, provoke and nibble, reasoning that its opponent will not answer with anything that could lead to the unthinkable.

It is important to be precise about what this claims. It does not say that nuclear weapons cause small wars, which have many causes and were common long before such weapons existed. It says only that mutual deterrence can lower the perceived risk of low-level aggression and so remove one brake on it. Nor does the paradox operate automatically. Its force depends on how confident each side is that escalation can be controlled. Where leaders doubt that a skirmish can be kept small, the old fear returns, and with it some of the old caution.

The implication is uncomfortable for those who credit deterrence with keeping the peace. What deterrence may secure is not peace in general but the absence of one particular kind of war, while the violence that remains is pushed downward and outward, into contested borderlands and into the hands of proxies. That is no small achievement, given what the alternative might be, and nothing in the paradox implies that the world would be safer if the largest powers could once again contemplate fighting each other directly. But the achievement should be described accurately. A system that prevents catastrophe partly by making lesser conflicts safer to start is not a system of peace; it is a way of choosing which wars will be fought.

passage: Why are some countries rich and others poor? For several decades the question has been staged as a contest between two answers. One points to geography: to climate, soils, disease and distance from the sea, which shape what can be grown, how healthy workers are and how cheaply goods can be moved. The other points to institutions: to whether property is secure, contracts are enforced and rulers are constrained, which shape whether people find it worth their while to invest, innovate and trade. Each side has its favourite evidence, and each has scored points against the other.

The institutional camp's strongest card is the observation that geography changes slowly while fortunes can change fast. Two halves of a peninsula with the same climate, the same soils and, until the middle of the twentieth century, a shared history can diverge dramatically within a couple of generations once they are placed under different political systems. Institutionalists have also pointed to a pattern among formerly colonised regions: some of those that were relatively densely settled and prosperous five centuries ago are relatively poor today, while some that were thinly populated then are rich now. Geography did not flip in the interval. What changed, the argument goes, were the institutions that colonisers imposed, extractive where there was wealth and labour to seize, more inclusive where settlers came to live.

The geographers' reply is that these comparisons, however striking, do not dispose of their case. A landlocked country far from major markets pays more to export every tonne it produces, whatever its laws say, and a tropical region where malaria is endemic carries a burden of illness that good government can reduce but not abolish overnight. These are direct effects, and no amount of constitutional reform makes a mountain range easier to cross. Geographers add that the peninsula, however vivid, is a single case, and that a single case can show that institutions are capable of mattering without showing how much they usually matter across the wide run of countries.

What both camps tend to overlook is how much of their contest is artificial. The reversal story itself, read carefully, is a story about geography working through institutions. Colonisers chose to settle or to extract partly according to how likely they were to survive the local diseases, and the soils of some regions suited crops that were profitable to grow with coerced labour on large estates. The institutions that resulted were, in this sense, partly geographical in origin, even if they later took on a life of their own. To ask, as statistical exercises often do, how much of the variation in income is due to geography and how much to institutions is to treat as rival causes what are frequently links in a single chain. The exercise can produce a number, but the number answers a question that the history does not pose.

None of this restores geography as destiny. The institutionalists are right that the same land can support very different outcomes, and that a country is not condemned by its latitude. The point is rather that the question 'which matters more?' should give way to the question 'how did they combine here?', which has a different answer in different places and cannot be settled by a single coefficient. For one country the answer may lie largely in a coastline that made trade cheap long before anyone drafted a constitution; for another, in rules imposed by outsiders that outlived the conditions which first made them profitable.

passage: Every few years a new survey announces that trust in public institutions has fallen again. Respondents are asked how much confidence they have in parliament, the courts, the police or the press, their answers are averaged, and the declining line is offered as evidence of a crisis. The finding is treated as self-interpreting: less trust is bad, more trust is good, and the task of leaders is to restore it. Each step of that reasoning deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives.

Begin with what the question measures. A person asked how far she trusts the courts may be reporting her estimate of their competence, her view of their honesty, her approval of recent verdicts, or simply her mood about public life in general. Answers about quite different institutions tend to rise and fall together, which suggests that much of what is captured is a general disposition rather than a considered judgement about any particular body. Nor does the answer reliably predict conduct. People who tell interviewers that they distrust the courts continue to sign contracts that only courts can enforce, and people who profess little confidence in the health service continue to take the medicines it prescribes. If trust is fundamentally a matter of what we are prepared to rely on, the survey and the behaviour can come apart, and it is not obvious that the survey is the better witness.

A second difficulty is that falling trust is ambiguous even where it is real. It may mean that institutions have become less reliable. It may also mean that citizens have come to expect more of them, or that information about their failures, once hidden, now circulates freely. In the last case the decline records not a deterioration in the institution but an improvement in the public's knowledge of it. The philosophical point beneath this is simple and often forgotten: trust is valuable only when it is placed in what is trustworthy. A population that trusted a corrupt police force completely would not be enjoying a civic good; it would be making a mistake, and one that the corrupt would be glad to exploit. What we should want is not high trust but well-calibrated trust, trust that rises and falls with the reliability of its object.

This does not license complacency. Distrust, warranted or not, has consequences of its own. Citizens who doubt that taxes are spent honestly may be readier to evade them; communities that expect the police to be indifferent may stop reporting crimes, which in turn makes the police less effective and the distrust more justified. A decline in measured trust can therefore be the beginning of a spiral that no recalibration will halt by itself, because the institution's reliability depends partly on the cooperation that distrust withdraws. The point is not that the numbers are meaningless but that they cannot, on their own, tell us whether we face a failing institution, a better-informed public or a passing mood.

What would tell us more is evidence of a different kind: whether expressions of trust track independent measures of institutional performance over time, whether people who say they distrust an institution still rely on it when something important is at stake, and whether trust differs between those who have dealt with an institution directly and those who know it only by reputation. Such evidence is harder to gather than a single question repeated every few years, and it yields no simple line on a chart for commentators to lament. That is precisely its value.

passage: The word 'stress' entered the study of living things from the study of materials, where its meaning is reasonably exact: the internal force per unit area within a body subjected to a load. In engineering, stress is distinguished from strain, the deformation that the load produces, and both are distinguished from the load itself. When the word was borrowed to describe what happens to organisms under pressure, these distinctions did not travel with it. In ordinary speech, and in a good deal of research, 'stress' can refer to the demanding situation, to the bodily and emotional reaction it provokes, or to the relation between the two, and it is often far from clear which of these is meant. A survey announcing that most workers feel stressed may be measuring their workloads, their symptoms or their sense of being overwhelmed, and the headline rarely says which.

The slippage is not merely a matter of untidy usage. Consider the familiar claim that stress is bad for health. If stress means the reaction, and the reaction is defined partly by its harmful effects, the claim is close to true by definition. If stress means the demanding situation, the claim is plainly false as a generalisation, since many people meet heavy demands without harm and some appear to thrive on them. Only if stress means a particular relation, demands that exceed what a person believes they can manage, does the claim become a substantive hypothesis that could turn out to be wrong. Much popular discussion moves among these meanings without noticing, and so acquires the authority of the first reading and the scope of the second.

The same confusion shadows the more recent enthusiasm for 'good stress'. To say that some stress is beneficial may mean that some demanding situations are worth seeking out, which is uncontroversial; or that some physiological reactions to demand improve performance, which is plausible within limits; or that people who interpret their reactions as helpful fare better than those who do not, which is a specific claim requiring specific evidence. Advice built on the phrase often slides from the first meaning, which everyone accepts, to the third, which is the one actually being sold. Each of the three deserves to be judged on its own evidence, and the plausibility of the first lends nothing to the third.

It might seem that the remedy is to abandon the word altogether. That would be a mistake, and not only because ordinary language is not so easily reformed. The very breadth of the term has allowed researchers in physiology, psychology, sociology and medicine to recognise that they were studying related things, and it has drawn attention to connections, between working conditions and heart disease, say, that narrower vocabularies might have kept apart. Whole programmes of research, on bereavement, on unemployment, on the burdens of caring for a sick relative, found a common frame in it. A concept can be scientifically fruitful precisely because it is loose at the edges, so long as those who use it know where the looseness lies.

What the word cannot do is carry an argument by itself. The useful discipline is to ask, whenever a claim about stress is made, which of its meanings is in play, and whether the evidence offered supports the claim under that meaning or only under a different one. A finding about reactions does not automatically license advice about situations, and a finding about interpretations says little about either. Keeping the senses apart costs a few extra words; failing to keep them apart has cost a good deal of confusion, some of it in the very places where clarity matters most.

passage: Each summer, the arrival of the monsoon over the southern tip of the Indian peninsula is announced on a particular day, and the date is reported as if something had been observed to happen: the rains have come. Newspapers compare it with the long-term average, and a delay of a week becomes a story about anxious farmers and rising food prices. Behind the announcement, however, lies not an event but a decision. The monsoon has no sharp leading edge. Showers build over days or weeks, winds shift gradually, and early bursts of rain may be followed by long dry spells. To fix a single day, forecasters must apply criteria, thresholds of rainfall across a set of stations and of wind and cloud, chosen so that the date can be determined consistently from one year to the next.

Calling the onset a convention is not to call it arbitrary. Good criteria pick out a real change in the behaviour of the atmosphere, and fixing them in advance prevents the date from being adjusted to suit hopes or headlines. A consistent definition also makes years comparable, so that researchers can ask whether onsets have tended to come earlier or later over many decades. Conventions of this kind are the ordinary machinery of science; the point at which a heavy shower counts as an extreme rainfall event, or a tropical storm as a cyclone, is fixed in the same way.

The trouble begins when the convention is mistaken for the thing it marks. A declared onset tells a farmer that a threshold was crossed somewhere along the coast; it does not tell her whether the soil in her own district holds enough moisture for seed to survive the next fortnight. In some years the rains, having satisfied the criteria, stall for weeks, and farmers who sowed on the strength of the announcement watch their seedlings wither. The date did nothing wrong; it was simply asked to answer a question it was never designed to answer.

The lesson is not that the onset date should be abolished, since it serves research and public communication reasonably well, but that a single number cannot serve every purpose at once. A measure built for comparing years across a century need not be the measure that should guide a decision about sowing next week. Agricultural advice would be better anchored in local indicators, such as accumulated rainfall and soil moisture in the district concerned, with the national date treated as background rather than as a signal to act. Definitions in climate science, like definitions elsewhere, should be judged by whether they fit the decision they are used to inform.

passage: When a country lowers its barriers to imports, the gains and the losses arrive in very different forms. The gains are spread thinly across millions of households, each of which pays a little less for clothing, appliances or food, usually without noticing why. The losses fall heavily on a few: the workers of a particular mill, the shops that depended on their wages, the town whose tax base was the mill. A small saving that nobody notices is politically weightless; a closed factory is a photograph on the front page. Those who lose know exactly what they have lost and whom to blame, while those who gain rarely connect their small savings to a decision taken in a distant ministry. It is not surprising that the politics of trade so often seems out of proportion to its economics.

Economists have a standard reply. Because the total gains exceed the total losses, the winners could in principle compensate the losers and still come out ahead, so that everyone ends up better off. The argument is correct as arithmetic, and it is the foundation of the case that open trade raises national welfare. But the word that carries the weight is 'could'. A compensation that is possible but never paid is no comfort to the people who bore the losses, and to present it as though it settled the matter is to confuse a hypothetical with a policy.

Where governments have tried to pay, the record is unimpressive, though the reasons are instructive. Programmes reserved for workers who could prove that their jobs were lost to imports required them to establish a cause that is often impossible to isolate, since a plant may close because of foreign competition, new machinery and poor management all at once. Many eligible workers never applied; many who applied were retrained for occupations that were themselves shrinking. The failure lay less in the idea of compensation than in tying it to a cause that could not be reliably identified.

This suggests that the better course is not a trade-specific remedy at all but support that follows the worker regardless of why the job disappeared: insurance against lost earnings, help with moving to where work exists, and training linked to employers who are actually hiring. Such measures cannot be justified as payment for trade alone, and they will cost more than narrow programmes did. Yet the case for open trade has always rested on the claim that its benefits are broadly shared. If that claim is to be more than an assertion, the sharing has to be done by someone, and it will not happen by itself.

passage: Astronomers cannot lay a measuring tape across the sky, and almost every distance beyond the nearest stars is therefore inferred rather than measured. The method is usually described as a ladder. At the bottom are stars close enough for their apparent shift against the background, as the earth travels around the sun, to be observed and converted into a distance by simple geometry. Among those stars are certain pulsating ones whose rhythm of brightening and fading is tied to their true brightness, so that once the rhythm has been timed, a comparison of true with apparent brightness yields a distance. Such stars can be picked out in nearby galaxies, where they in turn calibrate brighter markers still, among them a class of exploding stars that can be seen across a large part of the observable universe.

Critics of the ladder, and many popular accounts of it, dwell on its fragility. Every rung rests on the one beneath, so an error at the bottom is carried, and perhaps magnified, all the way to the top. A small mistake in the geometry of nearby stars would misplace the pulsating stars, which would misplace the exploding ones, which would in turn misplace the remote galaxies whose distances tell us how fast the universe is expanding. On this view the ladder is really a chain, and a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

The image is apt, but only half of it. A chain fails at its weakest link because each link is tested by nothing except the load it bears. The rungs of the distance ladder are tested by one another. Wherever two methods can both be applied to the same objects, their answers ought to agree, and when they do not, the disagreement points to a fault in one of them. Several of the largest revisions of cosmic distances in the past century came about in just this way, when a comparison between overlapping rungs exposed a hidden assumption, such as the neglect of dust that dims starlight or the confusion of two kinds of pulsating star with one. Interdependence, in other words, is not only a route by which errors travel upward; it is also the means by which they are caught.

This is no reason for complacency. Cross-checks catch only the errors that differ between methods; a mistake shared by every rung, or built into a calibration on which all of them rely, would pass each comparison untouched. That is why the present disagreement between the expansion rate measured with the ladder and the rate inferred from observations of the early universe is taken so seriously. It may expose a flaw common to the ladder's rungs, or it may reveal something new about the cosmos itself. Either outcome would be informative, and the fact that the question can be posed so sharply is itself a tribute to how far the ladder has been tightened. A structure that could not be checked could never have produced a disagreement worth arguing about.

passage: Every few years a new generation is given a name, and with the name comes a character. One cohort is said to be idealistic and later complacent, another cynical, another anxious, entitled or unusually attached to its telephones. The labels are used by marketers, journalists and employers with a confidence that would be remarkable in any other classification of human beings. We would hesitate to say that everyone born under a given star sign shares a temperament; we say something not very different, and with far less hesitation, about everyone born within a given span of fifteen years. The labels are also remarkably durable: once a cohort has been named and described, the description tends to follow it into middle age, revised only when a newer cohort arrives to take its place as the subject of worry.

The trouble begins with a problem of method that social scientists have long recognised. When one group of people differs from another, the difference may reflect their age (the young almost everywhere change jobs more often than the middle-aged), the period in which they are observed (everyone, of whatever age, was affected by a recession or a new technology), or the cohort into which they were born, meaning a lasting imprint left by the conditions of their early years. Only the last is a generational effect in the strict sense. But the three are bound together by arithmetic: a person's age is simply the current year minus the year of birth, so that once any two are known the third is fixed. No set of observations can by itself pull them apart; some assumption from outside the data is always required. Much of what is confidently attributed to a generation turns out, on inspection, to be what people of that age have always done, or what people of every age were doing at the time.

A second difficulty concerns boundaries. The years at which one generation is said to end and the next to begin are chosen by convention, and different sources disagree about them by several years. A person born on the last day of one span and a person born on the first day of the next are assigned different characters, while two people born fourteen years apart within one span are assigned the same. Differences within a labelled cohort, by class, region, education and much else, are typically far larger than the differences between cohorts, which is to say that the label groups people along the axis on which they least differ.

None of this shows that generations are a fiction. There is a serious idea buried under the marketing: that people who come of age during a war, a depression or a political upheaval may carry its mark for life, and may differ in lasting ways from those who met the same events earlier or later in their lives. Such effects have been found, and they are not trivial. But they are anchored to events rather than to calendars; they mark some members of a cohort far more deeply than others, depending on where and how the event touched them; and they rarely produce a single character that an entire cohort shares.

Why, then, do the calendar labels persist? Part of the answer is that they are convenient, turning a tangle of causes into a story with protagonists. Part of it is that they flatter, inviting each cohort to see itself as distinctive and its elders or juniors as the problem. The cost of the story is easy to miss. When young adults find housing unaffordable or work insecure, attributing their situation to a generational temperament converts a question about economic arrangements into a question about character, and a question about character has no obvious policy answer.

passage: The quarrel between advocates of green growth and advocates of degrowth is usually staged as a dispute about a single empirical question: can economic output keep rising while the pressure it places on the planet falls? Green growth answers yes. Rich economies, it observes, have already shown that output and emissions can move apart, as electricity is generated from cleaner sources, heavy industry gives way to services, and the same goods are made with less material. Degrowth answers no, or not fast enough. Some of the apparent separation, it replies, reflects production moved abroad rather than pollution avoided; much of the rest is merely relative, a fall in emissions per unit of output that is swamped by the growth of output itself. On this view the only reliable way for rich countries to shrink their ecological footprint is to shrink their economies, or at least to stop enlarging them.

Both sides are right about something, and the way they frame the dispute obscures what it is really about. That emissions and output can diverge in absolute terms is no longer a mere hypothesis; it has happened in a number of countries, even after allowing for the carbon embodied in their imports. But the existence of absolute decoupling settles less than its champions suppose. The relevant question is not whether emissions can fall while output rises but whether they can fall fast enough, given how little more carbon the atmosphere can absorb before the damage becomes severe. A rate of decline that would be impressive in almost any other context may still be far too slow in this one. Equally, the degrowth case proves less than its champions suppose. That past decoupling has been too slow does not show that it must remain so; the pace of change in energy technology has repeatedly surprised forecasters, and the costs of some forms of clean power have fallen faster than most people expected a generation ago.

The deeper difficulty is that both camps take GDP as the variable of interest, one wishing to keep it rising and the other to see it fall. Yet GDP is neither the cause of environmental damage nor its cure. It is a sum of market transactions, some of which burn fuel and clear land and some of which, such as teaching, nursing or repairing, do very little of either. An economy could grow while its emissions fell sharply, if the growth came from activities of the second kind; it could shrink while its emissions rose, if a recession struck services harder than it struck heavy industry. To make the size of GDP the target, in either direction, is to aim at a proxy that is only loosely tied to the thing that matters.

A more productive stance would be indifference to growth as such. Policy would set limits directly on what does harm, through carbon prices, caps on extraction and the protection of land, and then let output rise or fall as it will within those limits. Such a stance asks something uncomfortable of each side. Advocates of green growth would have to accept that if the limits prove binding, slower growth may be the price, and that this would be not a failure of policy but a possible result of it. Advocates of degrowth would have to accept that if the limits are met while output rises, there is no further environmental case for shrinking the economy, whatever other reasons they may have for wanting a different kind of society. Neither concession is trivial, which may explain why the debate is so seldom conducted on these terms.

passage: Critics of political language have long treated the slogan as its lowest form. A slogan, they point out, asserts nothing that could be checked. Words such as renewal, fairness, security or change are compatible with almost any programme, and a campaign that rallies behind one of them has, in effect, declined to say what it will do. On this account the vagueness of the slogan is a species of evasion, and the remedy is to demand specifics: costed proposals, timetables, named measures that a voter can hold against the candidate once the votes have been counted.

There is a good deal of sense in this, but it rests on a picture of the voter as an individual buyer comparing the contents of rival packages. Politics in most large societies does not work like that. A party seeking a majority must assemble people whose interests and hopes overlap only partly: the worker and the small employer, the city and the countryside, the young and the retired. A precise programme would divide them at once, since each specific measure pleases some members of the coalition at the expense of others. A slogan holds them together by offering a phrase into which each can read a version of what he or she wants. Its emptiness is not a failure of communication; it is what allows a heterogeneous coalition to communicate with itself at all.

To see the slogan in this way is not to absolve it, for the difficulty has merely been postponed. A coalition assembled on an open phrase must, once it wins, translate the phrase into decisions, and each decision closes off some of the readings that brought supporters in. Those whose reading is closed off do not usually feel that a compromise has been struck; they feel that a promise has been broken, and in a sense they are right, since the slogan let each of them believe that it had been made to them. The disillusionment that so regularly follows electoral victory is often attributed to the cynicism of politicians, but a good deal of it is built into the structure of the appeal. Vagueness borrows support from the future, and the future presents the bill.

Nor is the critics' remedy as clean as it looks. A detailed platform has its own dishonesty, of a quieter kind. It implies a control over events that no government possesses, and its specific commitments are routinely overtaken by a recession, a war or some crisis that no one foresaw. A voter who holds a government to the letter of such a platform may end up rewarding rigidity over judgement. Specificity, in other words, can be as much a performance as vagueness is, a display of seriousness staged for an audience that has learned to distrust slogans.

What, then, should a careful listener ask of political language? Not that it abandon general phrases, which coalitions cannot do without, nor that it supply a detailed plan for every contingency. A more useful question is whether the speaker, pressed on how the slogan would decide a real conflict between its own supporters, can name the principle that would settle it. A slogan backed by such a principle is simply a commitment stated at a high level of generality, and it can be held to account at that level. One that dissolves into a different answer for each audience that asks is merely a mirror, and it is the mirror, not the generality, that deserves the critics' contempt.
